Article Title: Tensions in Northern Ireland: Why the 30-year-old Garvaghy Road parade row is back
Article Text:
People block the Garvaghy road ahead of the Protestant Orange Drumcree parade. (Reuters photo)

Why did the latest confrontation happen?

Nigel Dawson, known as District Master of Portadown Loyal Orange Lodge, speaks to a police officer after police blocked the road near Drumcree Church (Reuters photo)

Why is one parade causing such a big dispute

The Orange Order represents a Protestant and British tradition.

The history behind Drumcree row

A person wears an Irish flag themed mask as people block the Garvaghy road (Reuters photo)

Why are politicians involved

Tensions remained high in Northern Ireland on Monday after police prevented members of the Orange Order from marching along the Garvaghy Road in Portadown, despite the route being legally approved for the first time in nearly three decades.The stand-off followed a day of protests in which thousands gathered to block the road, while police kept the two sides apart.The dispute centres on the Drumcree parade, an annual march by the Orange Order, a Protestant organisation closely associated with British unionism.The march was supposed to pass through Garvaghy Road, a predominantly Catholic and Irish nationalist area of Portadown. The route had been banned since 1998 because previous attempts to use it had triggered serious unrest.Northern Ireland's Parades Commission had initially kept restrictions on the march, but a court challenge overturned the decision. The commission then allowed a much smaller parade of 35 people, without bands or supporters, and required it to start by 8am and finish by 9.30am. A final court challenge by residents was also rejected, clearing the way for the march.That decision immediately reignited opposition in Garvaghy Road.Around 2,000 people gathered there on Sunday and blocked the route. Members of Sinn Féin, including First Minister Michelle O'Neill and party leader Mary Lou McDonald, joined the protest. The Orange Order remained near Drumcree Parish Church, waiting for police to allow the route to be used.The stand-off continued into the early hours of Monday. A group of Orangemen attempted to move towards the road, but police Land Rovers blocked their way. Police also faced stone throwing from protesters and used tear gas to control the crowd.Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom, but its population has long been divided between two broad political identities. Unionists, who are predominantly Protestant, generally want Northern Ireland to remain part of the UK.Nationalists, who are predominantly Catholic, generally identify as Irish and support the idea of a united Ireland. Religion is therefore an important marker of the divide, but the deeper argument is about national identity and whether Northern Ireland should remain British or eventually become part of a united Ireland.The Orange Order represents a Protestant and British tradition. It says its marches are an important part of its cultural and religious heritage. But many Catholics and nationalists see some of these marches as provocative when they pass through their neighbourhoods. Garvaghy Road became one of the most sensitive examples of that dispute.Attempts by the Orange Order to march along Garvaghy Road became a major flashpoint during the Troubles, the decades of political and sectarian conflict in Northern Ireland.The confrontation was not simply about a parade. It reflected the much wider struggle between communities with competing British and Irish identities. Earlier Drumcree stand-offs were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings, making the route one of the most controversial in Northern Ireland.In 1998, the route was banned from the Orange Order's parade. That same year, the Good Friday Agreement helped bring an end to the main period of conflict known as the Troubles. The agreement established a new political framework based on power-sharing and recognised that Northern Ireland's constitutional status could ultimately change if its people voted for it. For nearly 30 years, the Orange Order was unable to complete the Drumcree route.This year's decision to allow the march therefore carried significance far beyond a few dozen people walking down a road. For Orangemen, it represented the restoration of a right they had been denied for decades. For many residents of Garvaghy Road, it revived memories of a conflict they believed had been left behind.The dispute has also exposed the continuing political divide at the heart of Northern Ireland. Sinn Féin party's Michelle O'Neill joined the protesters and urged them to "stay the course". Her participation angered unionist politicians, who argued that a senior government figure should not support a protest against a legally authorised parade.DUP leader Gavin Robinson accused O'Neill and other Sinn Féin politicians of being "lawmakers acting as lawbreakers".Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant has called for "compromise", while British and Irish leaders have urged calm. Police Chief Constable Jon Boutcher has also called on people with influence to help maintain a peaceful situation.The concern is not just about this particular march. The Drumcree dispute was once associated with some of the worst violence of the Troubles, so any confrontation carries a powerful historical memory.The current situation is therefore a clash between a legally approved Protestant parade, a Catholic nationalist community opposed to the route, and a police force trying to enforce the law without allowing the dispute to return to the violence of the past.
Article Summary: The dispute centres on the Drumcree parade, an annual march by the Orange Order. The march was supposed to pass through Garvaghy Road, a predominantly Catholic and Irish nationalist area of Portadown. The route had been banned since 1998 because previous attempts to use it had triggered serious unrest.

Article Title: In 2005, Walmart pledged to protect one acre for every acre it developed; 21 years later, the programme has helped protect more than 2.2 million acres
Article Text:
Representative Image of Walmart's commitment to wildlife conservation, highlighting the protection of 2.2 million acres (AI Generated Image)

How Walmart's Acres for America programme began in 2005

Acres for America has protected more than 2.2 million acres

2026 Acres for America grants will protect more than 177,000 acres

The programme now works through local conservation projects

In 2005, Walmart made a commitment to help permanently conserve one acre of wildlife habitat in the United States for every acre of land developed by its stores. Twenty-one years later, the Acres for America programme has supported 138 projects that have permanently protected more than 2.2 million acres across all 50 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico. The programme is a partnership between Walmart and the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, or NFWF, and its latest figures show $73.6 million in Walmart funding and more than $1 billion in total conservation impact. The effort has continued through successive 10-year commitments, with seven new grants announced in 2026.Acres for America began in 2005, when Walmart made a 10-year, $34.5 million commitment to NFWF to purchase and preserve one acre of wildlife habitat for every acre of land developed by Walmart. The programme's current materials describe its original conservation goal as approximately 100,000 acres, which it has now surpassed by more than 20 times.The programme was designed around four broad objectives: protecting critical habitat for birds, fish, plants and wildlife; connecting existing protected lands; providing opportunities for people to enjoy the outdoors; and supporting communities whose economies depend on forestry, ranching and recreation.Walmart renewed the programme for another decade in 2015 and announced a further 10-year, $34.5 million renewal with NFWF in November 2024. Walmart said that the latest commitment, combined with previous contributions, brought its total contributions to NFWF through the programme to more than $100 million.The programme's current figures show how far it has moved beyond its original target. NFWF's 2026 grant slate says Acres for America has funded 138 projects across all 50 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico and permanently protected more than 2.2 million acres. A separate April 2026 NFWF release says Walmart's $73.6 million investment has generated more than $1 billion in total conservation impact, including matching contributions.The projects have also helped connect millions of acres of protected land, supporting larger conservation landscapes and wildlife movement. The programme has provided nearly $4 million in emergency response funding connected to the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in 2010 and Hurricane Sandy in 2012. It has also invested more than $1.8 million in community-based projects in cities including New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, San Diego, Denver, Bridgeport, Portland, Albuquerque and Washington, D.C.The latest round of funding adds seven projects across California, Colorado, Kansas, New Mexico, North Carolina, Oklahoma and Virginia. NFWF announced $5.4 million in grants in April 2026, with the projects expected to protect more than 177,000 acres. The awards are backed by $135.8 million in matching contributions, producing a stated total conservation impact of $141.2 million.Among the projects, the New Mexico Land Conservancy will use an $800,000 grant to help permanently protect the 19,316-acre Ghost Ranch and five miles of Rio Chama frontage through a conservation easement that guarantees public access. In Oklahoma, The Conservation Fund received $650,000 toward protecting 11,333 acres as the state's first official State Forest, including habitat for the threatened leopard darter and federally threatened and endangered mussels. In Colorado's San Luis Valley, Western Rivers Conservancy received $535,000 toward conserving 45,952 acres at the headwaters of the Rio Grande, including more than 30 miles of perennial cold-water streams supporting native Rio Grande cutthroat trout.Acres for America does not operate as a single land-buying project. Its grants support conservation organisations, land trusts and other partners carrying out individual projects around the country. The 2026 slate includes conservation easements, land acquisitions and transfers to public agencies, depending on the location and conservation goal.That structure allows the programme to support very different landscapes, from ranchland and prairie to forests, river headwaters and wildlife habitat. The 2026 projects alone include a multigenerational ranch in the Flint Hills of Kansas and Oklahoma, mountain conservation in North Carolina, the Cumberland Highlands in Virginia and a cattle and sheep ranch in northeastern California. With the latest grants, a pledge that began in 2005 with a target of roughly 100,000 acres has grown into a programme reporting more than 2.2 million acres permanently protected across the United States and its territories.
Article Summary: 2026 Acres for America grants will protect more than 177,000 acres. The programme is a partnership between Walmart and the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, or NFWF. Walmart made a 10-year, $34.5 million commitment to preserve one acre of wildlife habitat for every acre of land developed by Walmart.

Article Title: Wyoming spent $1.8 million to buy an 80-year-old hot-springs water park inside a state park; after closing it, officials may now spend another $1 million to demolish almost everything
Article Text:
Wyoming Hot Springs LLC, owned by former Alaska Sen. Mark Begich, is taking over operations at several park properties. The company has already taken possession of the former Hellie's TePee Pools and is scheduled to take over the Hot Springs Hotel on Oct. 31.

A costly decision

New operator faces bigger challenge

A century of history

Tourism impact

For generations, Star Plunge has been part of the rhythm of Thermopolis, Wyoming, where tourists arrive for the mineral-rich waters of Hot Springs State Park and locals have watched the aging water park evolve around them. Now, the historic attraction has reached an uncertain turning point, after Wyoming spent nearly two years and $1.8 million to regain control of the property, the state may have to spend up to another $1 million simply to tear much of it down, states an online report by Cowboy State Daily. As per the report, the facility is facing serious electrical and structural problems, along with reported gas leaks and sagging support beams. State officials are now weighing whether repairing the aging complex makes financial sense or whether starting over with a new attraction would be the better option.According to the online report, Star Plunge was purchased by the state as part of a settlement involving former owner Roland Luehne. Wyoming had hoped the acquisition would clear the way for a broader effort to revive the aging amenities at Hot Springs State Park.Instead, inspections following the closure uncovered problems that were more extensive than initially expected. State officials have estimated demolition alone could approach $1 million. Rebuilding a replacement facility could cost several million dollars more, while a major renovation of the existing structure could also require a multimillion-dollar investment.The final decision is expected to depend partly on assessments from the state fire marshal and electrical inspectors, as well as discussions with the park's incoming concessionaire.Wyoming Hot Springs LLC, owned by former Alaska Sen. Mark Begich, is taking over operations at several park properties. The company has already taken possession of the former Hellie's TePee Pools and is scheduled to take over the Hot Springs Hotel on Oct. 31. The operator has committed several million dollars toward renovations across the properties, but any major rebuilding or renovation of Star Plunge would fall largely within that future concession arrangement.The state's initial hope had been to address basic safety issues and reopen Star Plunge quickly. The newly discovered problems have made that scenario increasingly unlikely.According to the report, Star Plunge traces its roots to 1900, decades before Hot Springs State Park was established in 1929. Luehne's family acquired the water park in 1975 and spent years adding features, including a new roof, a vapor cave and multiple water slides. Among its signature attractions was the Super Star 500, which the family described as one of the longest water slides of its era. A tube slide followed in 1987, with a smaller baby slide added two years later.But decades of use also left their mark. Visitors increasingly complained about deteriorating slides, rust and other signs of aging, while state officials had expressed concerns about the condition of the park's amenities for years.The uncertainty comes at a difficult time for Thermopolis, whose tourism economy depends heavily on visitors drawn to its famous hot springs. Local short-term rental operators previously reported weaker traffic after Star Plunge closed, even with other pools remaining open.Elsewhere in the park, work is moving forward. A new boardwalk around the terraces is nearing completion, while negotiations for the Hot Springs Hotel are also approaching the finish line.For Star Plunge, however, the future could mean a transformed attraction—or the end of the historic structure altogether. State officials have made clear that the site will eventually have a water-based attraction again. What remains unknown is whether it will still be Star Plunge, rebuilt in a new form, or an entirely new facility rising where the old one stood.Image Courtesy: Cowboy State Daily
Article Summary: Star Plunge, a century-old water park in Thermopolis, Wyoming, has been closed for more than a year. Inspectors found electrical and structural problems, along with reported gas leaks and sagging support beams. Wyoming spent nearly two years and $1.8 million to regain control of the property. The state may have to spend up to another $1 million simply to tear much of it down.

Article Title: ‘We are being scapegoated’: Why refugees fear renewed anti-migrant violence in South Africa
Article Text:
A protest by March and March, an anti-immigration movement

'We’re not xenophobic; campaign is against undocumented migration'

How has the South African government responded

Poll Vote & Share your view What is the best way to reduce tensions around migration in South Africa? Stronger law enforcement Dialogue between communities 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A September 30 deadline declared by South Africa's March and March, an anti-immigration movement that has led anti-migrant protests across the country this year, has renewed fears of violence among migrant communities.Refugees are also fearing fresh unrest as South Africa will hold local government elections on November 4, with migration emerging as an increasingly prominent political and social issue.“I am in hiding now because they say they are going to kill me for speaking about the rights of foreigners,” Al Jazeera quoted Bishop Raphael Bahebwa, a refugee from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), as saying.Bahebwa has lived in South Africa for 26 years and has witnessed repeated flare-ups of anti-foreigner sentiment. But he says this year feels “different.”“It has been very tough. Never before have I experienced something like this,” he added.According to Kafuti Muyumba, another refugee from the DRC, many members of the refugee community were “afraid” to return to neighbourhoods where they had built businesses and lives. Muyumba, a small business owner and representative of the refugee community, said tensions had left many "fearful" for their safety.“People are afraid. Even the police allow March and March violence. They came with sticks and say we are attacking them. This is not the first time we are experiencing xenophobia. In 2008 and then in 2015 we also experienced this,” Muyumba stated.In 2008, xenophobic violence spread through townships and informal settlements across South Africa, killing dozens of people and displacing thousands. Further outbreaks of violence against foreign nationals followed in subsequent years.March and March has described its mobilisation as a "campaign against undocumented immigration, crime and deteriorating conditions in South African communities," while arguing that the South African government’s response to immigration enforcement has been “insufficient”.The group has called for undocumented foreigners to leave South Africa and warned of further demonstrations if its demands are not met.Its leaders have repeatedly rejected accusations that the campaign is xenophobic, insisting that its target is undocumented migration rather than foreign nationals generally.March and March maintains that its sole demand is for undocumented immigrants to leave South Africa and return to their home countries.In response to the ongoing protests, the South African government has intensified immigration enforcement.Between June 14 and August 20, authorities processed 86,596 foreign nationals for deportation and repatriation, according to the government’s Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration.Malawians made up the largest group, followed by Zimbabweans and Mozambicans.Government data indicates that 90% of those repatriated had entered South Africa illegally, while 95% were classified as having crossed the border outside official ports of entry.The government maintains that the operations form part of a broader effort to strengthen border management and enforce immigration law.At the same time, officials have repeatedly warned private groups against taking immigration enforcement into their own hands.March and March’s September 30 deadline has no legal authority. The government maintains that ordinary citizens cannot deport anyone from South Africa.However, deadlines do not need legal force to create fear, as was the case for an earlier deadline of June 30."They are scapegoating us as foreigners. It is not going to end on September 30. It has to do with the elections," Bahebwa said.
Article Summary: March and March has declared a September 30 deadline for undocumented immigrants to leave South Africa. The deadline has renewed fears of violence among migrant communities. South Africa will hold local government elections on November 4. The government has intensified immigration enforcement in response to the protests.

Article Title: Over 30 killed in 3 separate attacks overnight in South Africa shootings; manhunt launched
Article Text:
A police officer is seen at a scene of a mass shooting at a house party in KwaMakhutha township

Four killed in Khayelitsha shooting

10 killed at Western Cape entertainment venue

South Africa police have launched a manhunt after three separate shootings across the country left more than 30 people dead and several others injured overnight, as authorities grapple with persistent violent crime.In the deadliest incident, 17 people were killed and 15 wounded after eight unidentified gunmen opened fire at a tavern in Wedela township in the West Rand District outside Johannesburg on Saturday evening, police said.According to police, patrons were drinking inside and outside the tavern when the suspects arrived and opened fire on those outside before entering the establishment and continuing to shoot.The attackers were allegedly armed with pistols and AK-47 rifles. Police said they also searched some patrons and took their mobile phones before fleeing in two unidentified vehicles, CNN reported.Police have launched a search for the suspects, but no arrests have been reported so far.Police were also investigating a quadruple murder following a shooting in Khayelitsha township in the Western Cape at around 7.15pm on Saturday.Three men with multiple gunshot wounds were found at the scene.Two victims were discovered inside a vehicle, while another was found beside it. All three were declared dead at the scene.A fourth victim, who had also suffered gunshot wounds, was taken to a medical facility but died upon arrival, police said.No suspect has been identified or arrested, and the motive remains unknown.In a separate incident, 10 people were shot dead at an entertainment venue in Lwandle township in South Africa’s Western Cape province early Sunday, police said.Gunmen reportedly entered the venue and opened fire on patrons. Five people died at the scene, while five others succumbed to their injuries in hospital.The latest attacks come amid concerns over persistent violent crime in South Africa. Experts have said mass shootings are becoming increasingly common, particularly in poorer communities.
Article Summary: 17 people killed and 15 wounded after eight unidentified gunmen opened fire at a tavern in Wedela township in the West Rand District outside Johannesburg. In a separate incident, 10 people were shot dead at an entertainment venue in Lwandle township in South Africa’s Western Cape province.

Article Title: Russia backs India's claim to UNSC seat, firmly shuts door on Germany & Japan
Article Text:
Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly (Photo: Reuters).

Russia on Saturday backed a permanent seat for India and Brazil on the United Nations Security Council, while strongly opposing the same for Western countries.During his speech at the General Assembly, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said no additional seats at the UNSC should be given to Western countries, especially to Germany and the US ally, Japan.Russia has been one of the most consistent supporters of India’s bid for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council . Moscow has repeatedly backed India’s candidature as part of a broader push to make the Council more representative of Asia, Africa and Latin America.Lavrov has previously argued that the current composition no longer reflects today’s global balance and explicitly endorsed India, alongside Brazil, for permanent membership.This support was reiterated in the 2026 BRICS New Delhi Declaration, with China and Russia backing India and Brazil for a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council.Lavrov accused the West of continuously pumping weapons into Ukraine while helping target drones and missiles at Russia's civilians and civilian infrastructure.He also mentioned that Europe raised an anti-Moscow regime in Kyivv, in order to control the Russian influence."To pursue a utopian goal of containing Russia, the West dismantled the European security system and cultivated a Russophobic regime in Kyiv," he said, while warning the Western nations of "consequences".He further accused Europe of doing everything to block a peaceful settlement with Ukraine and disrupt negotiation prospects favoured by many, including the Trump administration.Lavrov claimed several EU leaders of being infected with racial superiority, encouraging the rise of what he called Ukrainian Nazism.The Russian foreign minister said the UN’s core principles were being put at risk, with the West overlooking the spread of Nazism in Ukraine.
Article Summary: Russia has been one of the most consistent supporters of India's bid for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council. Moscow has repeatedly backed India’s candidature as part of a broader push to make the Council more representative of Asia, Africa and Latin America.

Article Title: ‘We will die’: Oleshky civilians eat weed to survive in Russian-held Ukrainian city
Article Text:
Smoke rises in Kyiv following a Russian jet-powered drone strike

The Guardian

The Guardian

Residents survive on one meal a day

The Guardian

Four tonnes of aid dropped by drones
