Ukraine’s Russian-occupied city of Oleshky is facing starvation, with around 2,000 civilians, including nearly 50 children, reportedly stranded as food supplies run out and evacuation efforts remain stalled,reported.A woman trapped in the city toldthat she had lost more than 40kg since the war began and was struggling to find enough food. “Right now, I’ve got absolutely nothing to eat,” she said, adding that the home where she spent last winter had been destroyed and burned.Oleshky, located across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson, has been described by Ukrainians familiar with the situation as a “hell on earth”.Food supplies to Oleshky reportedly began drying up after May as Russian forces expanded minefields and drone coverage around the city, making deliveries increasingly difficult.Residents toldthey were sometimes surviving on just one meal a day — soup without potatoes, made from courgettes grown in former apartment flower boxes, and occasionally supplemented with foraged purslane, an edible weed.Kherson’s military authorities carried out a large-scale drone operation over the weekend, dropping emergency food, water and medical supplies across Oleshky and nearby villages.According to the Kherson military governor’s office, about four tonnes of food were dropped at 100 locations. However, it remained unclear how much of the aid was intercepted by Russian forces.Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha raised the situation in Oleshky at the UN General Assembly this week, warning of a “humanitarian catastrophe” and calling for the immediate evacuation of civilians.A food convoy heading towards Oleshky on September 1 was attacked, with Moscow blaming Ukrainian forces and Kyiv blaming Russian troops.
Article Summary: Around 2,000 civilians, including nearly 50 children, are stranded in Oleshky. Food supplies have run out and evacuation efforts remain stalled. A woman trapped in the city said she had lost more than 40kg since the war began and was struggling to find enough food.

Article Title: White House posts third taxpayer-paid ad campaign boosting Trump ahead of midterm elections
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump

Three ads, same spotlight

Taxpayer money under scrutiny

White House pushes back

What the law says

Trump's political rhetoric is back on TV screens, this time in taxpayer-funded White House ads."Final Battle," a 30-second spot, is the third government-funded ad to air in recent days. While the White House has referred to the ads as public service announcements, Democrats and former ethics officials question whether they amount to political advertising that could breach federal rules on the use of taxpayer money.The latest ad shows black-and-white footage of Trump walking through a hallway lined with portraits while his voice plays over the images. Its visuals and rhetoric echo a video he posted on Truth Social in January 2024, during his third presidential campaign.The US President said that the country must expel "the warmongers," "globalists" and "deep state" actors from government and remove his political opponents from power."We will cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists," he said. "We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all."The ad is nearly identical to most of the original, which had an extra six seconds featuring Trump's campaign logo and a number to text.The government version instead ends with "Paid for by the US Government" across the screen.According to ad-tracking firm AdImpact, it aired over the weekend during "Saturday Night Live", "Fox News Sunday" and several college and NFL football games. It ran during at least two NFL games on Sunday: Fox's broadcasts of Commanders-Seahawks and Panthers-Browns.More than $300,000 has been spent on it. It is unclear which government agency produced and paid for the ads.The push comes just over a month before the November midterms.The Trump administration appeared to step up its use of taxpayer-funded television spots promoting President Donald Trump.The latest, a minute-long ad, features scenic footage of Mount Rushmore at night along with quotes and clips from Trump's Fourth of July weekend speech there marking the country's 250th anniversary. It was the second government-funded TV ad to air in three days, while spending on the first had risen to at least $443,000.Lawmakers from both parties criticised the first ad on Thursday, questioning its legality and appropriateness given its political nature, its timing ahead of the November midterms and the use of taxpayer money.The first ad, which began airing Wednesday, featured rapidly edited pictures and videos of Trump, with audio of him denouncing communism and socialism. On-screen text highlighted his administration's achievements, including "reigniting American manufacturing".The White House had posted the ad on X on September 26 with the caption "America will NEVER be a communist country."Several Democratic members of Congress sent a letter last week to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, calling on the administration to stop airing the ads.Common Cause has also questioned the spending."I don't think you have to be a legal scholar and wonder why the president has to use taxpayer funds to promote his image" this close to an election, Carol Evans, the group's vice president for policy, told CNN.Republican Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana also questioned the use of public money for image-building ads."I don't think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves," he told CBS News.His comments follow a $200 million-plus campaign run last year by the department of homeland security under then-secretary Kristi Noem. The ads prominently featured her on horseback, warning that people who broke US laws would be "hunted down and deported".Under questioning from Kennedy in March, Noem testified that Trump had approved the campaign. Trump later criticised the spending and, not long afterwards, fired her.A White House spokesperson said, "The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic. We should be proud of our country."The White House has maintained that the ads promote national pride. It argues they are not campaign ads because Trump is not on the ballot and the spots contain no call to action. It says its commercials "are very clearly not campaign ads."It points to government-funded advertising under George W Bush, Barack Obama, Joe Biden and earlier administrations as examples of public money being used to explain policies. It cites campaigns on Medicare, Obamacare and Covid-19 vaccination."When prior Administrations utilized the airwaves, it was called 'public education,'" it said. "When this Administration promotes pride in our country, many of those same voices call it 'propaganda.'" Communications director Steven Cheung posted on X on Sunday, "Don't let the Fake News get away with their lies about our epic Public Service Announcements that have been running on tv."Federal law, enacted annually in appropriations bills since the 1950s, prohibits agencies from using taxpayer money for unauthorised "publicity or propaganda".The Government Accountability Office (GAO), Congress's investigative arm, has interpreted the rule as covering purely partisan communications. It also recognises that administrations can use public money to explain and defend their policies.However, the GAO previously found that one of the earlier advertising campaigns the White House cites had violated the anti-propaganda law.
Article Summary: Third government-funded ad to air in recent days. Democrats and former ethics officials question whether they amount to political advertising. White House says ads are not campaign ads because Trump is not on the ballot and spots "are very clearly not ads" It points to government ads under George W Bush, Barack Obama, Joe Biden as examples of public money being used to explain policies.

Article Title: Florida’s python team followed 40 tagged male snakes and ended the season with 177 Burmese pythons removed and more than 4,100 eggs taken from the ecosystem
Article Text:
Florida Burmese python removal began with a 17-foot female

How Florida's python removal programme uses tagged scout snakes

More than 4,100 eggs were removed

Florida python programme removed 8,080 pounds of snakes

The programme has been running since 2013

Burmese python removal continues across southwest Florida

A season of tracking Burmese pythons across the difficult terrain of southwest Florida ended with 177 snakes removed and more than 4,100 eggs taken out of the ecosystem. The work, carried out by the Conservancy of Southwest Florida and its python action team, covered about 200 square miles of Collier County between November 2025 and April 2026, as reported by the Conservancy of Southwest Florida. Together, the captured snakes weighed 8,080 pounds, or just over four tons. The programme has been running for more than a decade, using radio-tagged male pythons to locate breeding snakes in places that can be difficult for people to reach. This season produced the largest total biomass removed by the organisation since the programme began in 2013.The first capture came in November, when a tagged male known as Snaquan led the tracking team to a large female python. She measured 17 feet and weighed 148 pounds, setting the tone for a season in which several of the snakes recovered were substantial animals.By April, the team had removed 177 Burmese pythons from the study area. The females captured during the season averaged about 95 pounds, while the heaviest reached 153 pounds. Several measured more than 16 feet.For the people following them through the landscape, size was only part of the challenge.Large females can spend time in remote areas, making them difficult to locate without a way of narrowing down where they are moving.The Conservancy's method centres on radio telemetry and a group of around 40 tagged male pythons. These animals are used as what the organisation calls scout snakes. During the breeding period, researchers monitor their movements. When a tagged male begins spending time around other pythons, the location can point the team towards a mating group. That allows biologists to reach the area and search for additional snakes, including females carrying eggs.It is a very different approach from simply searching for snakes across the Everglades landscape. The tagged animals provide a moving signal, helping researchers decide where to concentrate their efforts. Ian Bartoszek, a wildlife biologist and science project manager with the Conservancy, said, “This was our first four-ton removal season. Our tagged scout snakes helped us locate large breeding snakes deep in the landscape before they had a chance to lay eggs. ”According to Conservancy of Southwest Florida, the programme's work this season extended beyond adult snakes with more than 4,100 python eggs also removed. The reproductive figures found inside captured females give some indication of why the team pays particular attention to breeding animals. Females examined during the season carried an average of about 70 eggs, according to the Conservancy.Some of the snakes had also been feeding on native animals. The organisation reported that around a quarter of the females captured contained remains of white-tailed deer. Burmese pythons are established in southern Florida, where their presence has raised concerns about predation on native wildlife. The Conservancy's work is aimed in part at reducing reproduction by finding breeding females and removing them before they can produce another generation.The scale of some captures means the fieldwork is not simply a matter of picking up a small reptile and carrying it away. Several females recovered during the season weighed well over 100 pounds. Photographs from the programme show researchers working with large snakes found after scout males were tracked through southwest Florida. Reportedly, one of the snakes located by scout number 103, known as Lincoln, measured 16 feet and weighed 140 pounds.The largest female captured during the season weighed 153 pounds. Snaquan's first lead had produced a 148-pound female. These individual animals account for a significant portion of the total biomass removed. Across all 177 snakes, the combined weight reached 8,080 pounds.The latest season brought the programme's cumulative total to about 1,750 Burmese pythons removed since it began in 2013. Those snakes have weighed more than 53,000 pounds altogether. The project has also generated research beyond the individual captures. The Conservancy said its work has contributed to 25 scientific publications examining areas such as python behaviour, habitat use and reproduction.The organisation works with several research partners, including the Rookery Bay National Estuarine Research Reserve, the US Geological Survey, the University of Florida and the South Florida Water Management District. The programme is funded through a combination of private donations, grants and conservation organisations.The end of the April field season does not mean Burmese python sightings have stopped. The Conservancy continues to ask people in the area to report snakes so they can be assessed and, where appropriate, removed. For the Conservancy's tracking team, the next stage will build on information collected during another breeding season. Each tagged scout snake adds to the understanding of where pythons move and how they use the landscape.The 2025-26 season ended with 177 adult snakes removed, thousands of eggs taken out and more than four tons of python biomass recorded. The figures now form part of a much longer effort that has been underway in southwest Florida for more than 13 years.
Article Summary: The Conservancy of Southwest Florida has been tracking Burmese pythons in southwest Florida for more than a decade. This season produced the largest total biomass removed by the organisation since the programme began in 2013. The largest female captured during the season weighed 153 pounds. More than 4,100 python eggs also removed.

Article Title: Drugged with ketamine, raped for hours: Ex-student sues Cornell University, 7 fraternity members
Article Text:
Ex-Cornell student sues university and 7 frat members, alleging she was drugged and raped for hours.

What does the lawsuit allege?

What happened after the alleged assault?

What did Cornell University say?

Why were no criminal charges filed?

What did Chi Phi fraternity and sexual violence support groups say?

A former student of Cornell University has filed a lawsuit against the institution and seven members of its Chi Phi fraternity, alleging that she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in October 2024. The woman, identified as Jane Doe in court documents, was 20 years old at the time of the alleged assault and has accused the university and fraternity members of failing to protect her and prevent the incident.The lawsuit, filed on September 16 in the New York Supreme Court, alleges that the woman was sexually assaulted by fraternity members at the Chi Phi house in Ithaca. According to the complaint, two fraternity members allegedly pressured her into snorting what they claimed was ketamine before sexually assaulting her. The complaint further alleges that a message was circulated in a fraternity Snapchat group chat, following which more men arrived and participated in the alleged assault.The woman reported the incident to Cornell University's police department around three weeks later, following which the university initiated an internal investigation. Her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, said that only two of the seven accused fraternity members were expelled, while others received lesser disciplinary penalties.He also claimed that none of the accused were arrested. The Tompkins County District Attorney's Office, however, said it reviewed the police investigation but found insufficient evidence to support criminal charges.The lawsuit accuses Cornell University and the fraternity members of breach of contract, negligence and violations of state law. The former student, who left the university following the alleged assault, is seeking compensatory and punitive damages. Cornell has said that its internal investigation was conducted in accordance with university policies and that the Chi Phi chapter remains barred from campus.According to the complaint, the former student, identified only as Jane Doe, was attending Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, when the alleged assault took place on October 19, 2024.She allegedly visited a friend at the Chi Phi fraternity house after drinking at her sorority and a nightclub. The lawsuit claims that she was intoxicated when she arrived at the house late that night.Two fraternity members allegedly pressured her into snorting a substance they identified as ketamine before sexually assaulting her.The complaint further alleges that one of the men subsequently sent a message in a Snapchat group chat named “Chi Phi Actives”, suggesting that a woman was available for sex.According to a report by WBNG, the lawsuit claims the message read, “free p----” upstairs.”Following the message, more fraternity members allegedly arrived at the house and participated in the assault, which the complaint says continued until around 5.45 am.The allegations have not been established in court.The former student reportedly approached Cornell University's police department approximately three weeks after the alleged incident and filed a report.The university subsequently initiated an internal investigation into the allegations, which involved at least 12 hearings, according to her attorney.Giuffra claimed that out of the seven fraternity members accused, only two were expelled, while the others received lesser disciplinary action, including suspensions, workshops or assignments requiring them to submit essays."Not one of these guys was arrested. Not one. That I can tell you for a fact," Giuffra said.The attorney also questioned the university's handling of the matter, alleging that several people could have intervened to prevent the assault."There were so many people that could have prevented it and they didn't," Giuffra said. "I've never seen anything like it."The former student subsequently left Cornell University following the alleged incident."She's not in college anymore because of this," Giuffra said. "She's barely hanging on for what these guys did to her."Cornell University acknowledged the allegations in November 2024, describing reports of drug abuse and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house as “abhorrent” and stating that such behaviour could not be tolerated within its community.Following the filing of the lawsuit, the university issued another statement on September 21, saying it was aware of the case involving allegations of sexual assault among members of the student community in 2024.The university said:"The Cornell Office of Civil Rights and the Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards investigated and adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies. The Xi chapter of Chi Phi fraternity remains barred from our campus."Federal privacy law prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students and we therefore are unable to make a public statement on any other disciplinary response. Violations of university policies could lead to sanctions up to and including suspension or expulsion. We will respond in detail through the legal process."Cornell also said it had established a task force on sexual assault following the investigation and introduced changes to address such incidents.The university has an online reporting platform through which students can report incidents involving bias, discrimination, harassment and sexual misconduct.The Tompkins County District Attorney's Office said it had reviewed the police investigation but determined that the available evidence was insufficient to pursue criminal charges.The office said it "conducted a thorough review of the police investigation," but "there was insufficient evidence to support criminal charges."The statement comes amid questions raised by the woman's attorney over the absence of arrests despite the university's internal disciplinary action against the accused fraternity members.The university's disciplinary proceedings and the criminal investigation are separate processes, with the former governed by university policies and the latter requiring sufficient evidence to pursue criminal charges.The lawsuit is now seeking to hold Cornell and the fraternity members legally accountable for the alleged assault and the circumstances surrounding it.The national headquarters of Chi Phi fraternity expressed concern over the allegations and said it condemns sexual violence. However, it declined to discuss the specific allegations while the lawsuit remains pending.In a statement to CBS News New York, the fraternity said:"The sexual assault allegations involving parties at Cornell University are deeply concerning. Anyone who reports sexual violence deserves to be heard and treated with compassion, dignity, and respect."Chi Phi unequivocally condemns sexual violence. Our founding principles of Truth, Honor, and Personal Integrity, and our mission of Building Better Men, call on every brother to demonstrate character through his actions and respect for the dignity and safety of others. Sexual violence is fundamentally incompatible with those expectations."We are aware of the lawsuit concerning an alleged incident in 2024. While we cannot discuss the specific allegations during pending litigation, we take this matter seriously. Our responsibility is to approach this with care for those affected and respect for a fair legal process."Meanwhile, Trae Banuelos-Rovaris of The Alliance Against Sexual Violence said support services were available for college students experiencing sexual assault and domestic violence."Gender-based violence is, you know, a global issue, and campuses are not immune," she said. "We have about 54 rape crisis centers that take funding just to work with college students alone."The lawsuit seeks monetary compensation, including compensatory and punitive damages, but does not specify the amount being sought. The case is pending before the court.
Article Summary: Former student sues university and 7 frat members, alleging she was drugged and raped for hours. The woman, identified as Jane Doe in court documents, was 20 years old at the time of the alleged assault. The lawsuit accuses Cornell University and the fraternity members of breach of contract, negligence and violations of state law.

Article Title: At 98, Iowa man Paul Little finally received his high school diploma 80 years after leaving school in 1946 to support his family
Article Text:
PC: YouTube

Paul Little left school before graduation to help support his family

PC: YouTube

Little gave thousands to help local students start their next chapter

A $50,000 gift brought his old school back into his life

Little was surprised with his diploma at his nursing home

PC: YouTube

His unfinished education later became a link to future graduates

Paul Little was supposed to leave Dallas Center High School in Iowa with his graduating class in 1946. Instead, circumstances at home meant school had to give way to work while he was still a junior. More than eight decades later, the qualification he never received was brought to him at the nursing home where he now lives. According to a CBS19 report, the 98-year-old was presented with a high school diploma on September 17, marking a school connection that had survived long after his own student days ended. By then, Little had spent decades farming, raised a family of his own and quietly put money towards young people in his local community.Little attended Dallas Center High School in Grimes, Iowa, and was on course to graduate in 1946. His education, however, stopped before he reached his final year. He left during his junior year because he needed to work and help support his family. There was no graduation ceremony for him and no diploma to take home. The decision belonged to a very different period of his life, when earning money could take precedence over finishing school.A little later built his working life around farming in nearby Guthrie County. The years passed, but the connection with education did not disappear entirely.Reportedly, he and his late wife, Eleanor, became supporters of local students and education programmes. Their involvement eventually extended beyond occasional contributions, with Little continuing to provide financial help to young people preparing for the next stage of their lives.As per a CBS19 YouTube video , Kasey Huebner, superintendent of the Panorama School District in Guthrie County, said, “For the last 15 to 18 years he’s given money out to help our kids get jump-started to the next stage in life”.The assistance was intended to help young people get started after school. His contributions came long after his own education had ended, making his relationship with local schools somewhat unusual. He had missed out on the final stage of his own secondary education, yet spent years helping students move forward with theirs.Little's support eventually reached the district where he had once attended school. After moving back to Dallas Center and becoming connected with the DCG Education Foundation, he offered financial backing for graduating seniors.According to the PEOPLE.com statement, “We were alerted to Paul’s story by the DCG Education Foundation. After moving back to Dallas Center, Paul connected with this group and offered financial support to our graduating seniors. Paul gave $50,000 to the DCG Education Foundation, and scholarships are now given out annually to our seniors.”The donation gave school officials another reason to look back at Little's long association with the community. Dallas Center-Grimes Community School District said Little's connection with the area stretches back almost eight decades. His financial support has become part of a scholarship programme that continues to benefit graduating students.For Little, the school was also the place where an unfinished part of his own education had begun. He had once been a pupil there, with graduation still ahead of him. Decades later, his return was tied not to a class reunion or a former-student event, but to the support he had provided to students following a path he had been unable to complete.On September 17, officials from the Dallas Center-Grimes Community School District visited Little at his nursing home and presented him with the diploma. It was a surprise visit, arranged after the district was alerted to his story by the DCG Education Foundation. Scott Blum, superintendent of the Dallas Center-Grimes Community School District, said, “We’re excited to play just a little role in recognizing the awesomeness that is a guy like Paul in our community. ”The diploma represented the education he had left behind as a teenager, but it also came with a more recent connection. By the time the school returned to that chapter of his life, Little had already spent many years helping students from the same wider community. The district described the honorary diploma as a way of thanking him for that contribution.Little did not return to education in the conventional sense. He did not complete the classes he had missed or return to school as an adult student. Instead, the school became part of his later life through his support for other young people. The district said his $50,000 donation has led to scholarships being awarded to seniors each year. That means the financial contribution made after his return to Dallas Center has a continuing link with students preparing to leave high school themselves. More than 80 years after he was supposed to graduate, school officials finally placed a diploma in his hands. This time, there was no unfinished school year waiting ahead of him.
Article Summary: Paul Little was supposed to leave Dallas Center High School in Iowa with his graduating class in 1946. He left during his junior year because he needed to work and help support his family. By then, Little had spent decades farming, raised a family of his own and quietly put money towards young people in his local community. After moving back to Dallas Center, he offered financial backing for graduating seniors.

Article Title: Rocky Hill-Glastonbury Ferry continues its historic Connecticut River service, carrying three cars at a time on a crossing that dates to 1655
Article Text:
pc: Connecticut Department of Transportation

How the ferry changed from horsepower to a diesel towboat

Rocky Hill-Glastonbury Ferry schedule and fares

PC: Connecticut Department of Transportation

How the ferry saves drivers nearly eight miles

A ferry has crossed the Connecticut River between Rocky Hill and Glastonbury since 1655, when the service began with a small raft pushed across the river using long poles. Over the centuries, the ferry has changed from horse-powered and steam-driven vessels to its current operation. Today, the three-car Hollister III, an open flatboat, is towed across the river by the diesel-powered Cumberland. The Rocky Hill-Glastonbury Ferry operates from April through November, providing a direct river crossing for motorists, pedestrians and cyclists. According to the Connecticut Department of Transportation, it is the oldest continuously operational ferry in the United States.The ferry has changed considerably since its early days. At one point, horses on treadmills in the centre of the craft provided the power needed to move it across the river. CTDOT's history of the ferry states that it was modernised in 1876, when the service moved to steam-driven craft.The ferry's current operation uses a different form of propulsion. CTDOT describes today's vessel as an open flatboat named the Hollister III, which can carry three cars. The barge is towed back and forth between the landings by Cumberland, a diesel-powered towboat.The ferry normally operates from April 1 through November 30.CTDOT lists operating hours of 7 a.m. to 6:45 p.m. from Monday to Friday, and 10:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. The ferry is closed on Thanksgiving, and weather conditions, water levels or mechanical issues can affect service.The ferry operates on demand rather than according to fixed departure times. CTDOT states that there are "no scheduled departure times" and that service is provided as vehicles and passengers arrive. Vehicles can board for $5 on weekdays and $6 on weekends, while pedestrians and cyclists pay $2 on all days, according to the department's current ferry information.The ferry provides a direct connection between Rocky Hill and Glastonbury at Route 160. CTDOT says motorists travelling between parts of southern Glastonbury and Rocky Hill can cut nearly eight miles one way from their journey by using the ferry. The department also identifies the crossing as particularly important for cyclists.Cyclists cannot use the Putnam Bridge on Route 2 between Wethersfield and northern Glastonbury, according to CTDOT. The department's ferry history page states that the Rocky Hill-Glastonbury Ferry is the only crossing available to cyclists between Hartford and Middletown, leaving a barrier of more than 13 miles without the ferry. High water near the landings delayed the April 1 start; CTDOT announced a May 1 opening. It was expected to welcome passengers through November.
Article Summary: The Rocky Hill-Glastonbury Ferry has been operating since 1655. It is the oldest continuously operational ferry in the United States. The ferry provides a direct connection between Rocky Hill and Glastonbury. Vehicles can board for $5 on weekdays and $6 on weekends, while pedestrians and cyclists pay $2 on all days.

Article Title: Jane Fonda conserved a New Mexico ranch before a 2018 easement protected 2,229 acres of habitat, farmland and nearly four miles of the Pecos River
Article Text:
PC: New Mexico Land Conservancy

How has Forked Lightning Ranch protected wildlife habitat over time

How did conservation easements protect Forked Lightning Ranch

PC:New Mexico Land Conservancy

What did the easement preserve at Forked Lightning Ranch

Forked Lightning Ranch, in the foothills of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains near Pecos, New Mexico, has passed through notable hands over decades. Texas oilman Buddy Fogelson bought it in 1941; after marrying actress Greer Garson in 1949, the ranch became known for entertaining guests. Following Fogelson's 1987 death, Garson donated part of the property to the National Park Service, forming part of Pecos National Historical Park. Jane Fonda purchased what remained in 2000 and worked to conserve its natural communities until selling it in 2015. A conservation easement, completed by the New Mexico Land Conservancy in 2018, later protected 2,229 acres, including nearly four miles of the Pecos River.After acquiring the remaining original ranch in 2000, Fonda worked to conserve and improve its natural communities. According to the New Mexico Land Conservancy, she continued this work until the property was sold to new owners in 2015.The Conservancy describes Forked Lightning Ranch as having important conservation values, including agriculture, scenic open space and wildlife habitat. The property also contains historic sites and includes nearly four miles of the Pecos River running through the ranch.The New Mexico Land Conservancy began protecting the ranch through conservation easements in three phases, starting in June 2010 and ending in October 2018. The Conservancy records the project as a donated conservation easement covering the ranch in San Miguel County.In October 2018, the Conservancy completed a new easement that added 403 acres to the existing protected area, bringing the total covered by the conservation easement to 2,229 acres. The new easement combined two previous easements with the additional acreage.The New Mexico Land Conservancy states that the easement protects the entire Forked Lightning Ranch and preserves the integrity of the property by removing the potential for selling off portions of the ranch in the future. The organisation identifies wildlife habitat, agricultural land and scenic open space among the property's conservation values.The Conservancy also notes that nearly four miles of the Pecos River run through the ranch and that several historic sites are located on the property. The completed 2018 easement therefore brought the previously protected areas and the additional 403 acres together under protection covering 2,229 acres of the ranch.
Article Summary: Forked Lightning Ranch is in the foothills of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains near Pecos, New Mexico. Texas oilman Buddy Fogelson bought it in 1941; after marrying actress Greer Garson in 1949, the ranch became known for entertaining guests. Jane Fonda purchased what remained in 2000 and worked to conserve its natural communities until selling it in 2015. A conservation easement, completed by the New Mexico Land Conservancy in 2018, later protected 2,229 acres, including nearly four miles of the Peco River.

Article Title: 'Would like to buy some?': Trump offered Xi US weapons as Washington sought to downplay Taiwan arms sale
Article Text:
Trump and Xi continued to discuss future US arms sales to Taiwan.

Taiwan arms package remains pending

US balancing ties with China & Taiwan

US President Donald Trump sought to downplay Washington's pending arms sale to Taiwan by telling Chinese President Xi Jinping that the US sells weapons to countries around the world, and even asking whether China would like to buy some, according to US ambassador to China David Perdue.“President Trump continues to say, hey, we sell arms to other people around the world. He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point,” Perdue told Fox News on Sunday.Perdue made the remarks days after Trump hosted Xi for a state visit in Washington. He did not specify when Trump made the comment or provide further details about the exchange.Perdue was speaking about US policy toward Taiwan, which has been waiting for months for Trump to approve a new arms package worth about $14 billion.Fox News host Shannon Bream had raised concerns from Republican and Democratic lawmakers about delays in US weapons orders and aid packages for Taiwan, which is seeking to strengthen its defences against a potential Chinese attack.Bream asked whether Washington was holding back arms sales to Taiwan to avoid angering Xi. Perdue rejected that suggestion, saying Trump “is as strong on Taiwan as I've ever seen anybody” and has already approved substantial weapons sales to the island.Earlier, Trump also sought to play down Taiwan as a major point of friction with Beijing, saying the issue did not feature prominently in his latest talks with Xi.“We didn't talk about Taiwan too much with Xi. Right now, it's, you know, fine. It's just moving along. Xi understands very much how I feel,” Trump told reporters.Trump and Xi met at the White House last week as Washington and Beijing sought to stabilise ties following months of tensions over trade, technology and other geopolitical issues.The summit resulted in an extension of the US-China trade truce, while differences over Taiwan, artificial intelligence and Iran remained.Taiwan has been waiting for months for Washington to approve a proposed arms package worth about $14 billion, following an $11 billion weapons deal announced last December.The latest package was put on hold after Trump’s meeting with Xi in Beijing in May. Trump has not indicated whether the deal will move forward following their latest summit.He had previously described arms sales to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China.Beijing has repeatedly urged Washington to halt arms sales to Taiwan, which China claims as part of its territory. Ahead of the latest summit, China had made clear that Taiwan remained a major issue in its talks with Washington.According to China’s official news agency Xinhua, Xi urged Trump to “prudently handle the Taiwan question” and called on Washington to oppose Taiwan independence. The White House did not immediately release its own account of the discussion on Taiwan.Earlier, Taiwan deputy foreign minister Chen Ming-chi said Washington “very much” understands the island’s defence requirements and the military pressure it faces from China.“Taiwan faces a severe situation in the Taiwan Strait. Even though China's economy is declining, it continues investing more resources into building military capacity. Under this context, the US very much understands our defence needs,” Chen said.“We do continuously communicate with them, and we believe the US understands the situation we face and our determination on defence investment completely,” he added.Chen also said Taiwan had repeatedly received assurances from Washington that its policy toward the island had not changed. Perdue separately told CNBC that there had been no change in Trump’s Taiwan policy, including on arms sales.Under US law, Washington is required to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself. The US does not formally recognise Taiwan as an independent country but remains its main informal security partner and arms supplier.At the same time, successive US administrations have left unclear whether Washington would directly intervene militarily if China attacked Taiwan.Beijing considers Taiwan part of China and opposes US arms sales to the island. Taiwan rejects China’s sovereignty claims and maintains that its future can be decided only by its people.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump sought to downplay Washington's pending arms sale to Taiwan. He told Chinese President Xi Jinping that the US sells weapons to countries around the world, and even asked whether China would like to buy some. Taiwan has been waiting for months for Washington to approve an arms package worth about $14 billion.

Article Title: ‘Will win very soon’: Trump hints at possible pre-midterm strikes on Iran
Article Text:
President Donald Trump on Iran war

Iran warns of ‘doomsday war’, keeps diplomacy open

Meet the Press

US President Donald Trump has expressed confidence that the US will “win” its war with Iran “very soon”, while leaving open the possibility of renewed military strikes before the upcoming US midterm elections.Speaking to Fox News on Sunday (local time), Trump said ending the conflict would trigger a sharp fall in global oil prices. He reiterated that preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon remains the primary US objective.“I think what's going to happen is we're going to win this war very soon, and as soon as we win it, the oil will go down, way down to what it was before the war,” Trump said.Asked whether US military strikes could resume before the midterm elections, Trump declined to rule out the possibility.“I don't want to say that. I don't want to say that. I mean, it's possible, but I just don't want to say that,” he said.Trump stressed that Iran must not be allowed to develop a nuclear weapon, calling nuclear deterrence “key to the whole thing”.Trump also claimed that Iran's economy had been severely damaged by the pressure campaign, saying, “They have no economy.” He pointed to the fall in the value of Iran's currency and rising prices, claiming inflation had reached nearly 300%, and citing a figure of 318%.Iranian foreign minister Seyyed Abbas Araghchi, meanwhile, said Tehran was prepared for a renewed conflict with Washington, while insisting that diplomacy remained an option.In an interview with NBC News', Araghchi said Iran was ready for a “doomsday war” and would defend itself against any new US aggression.“We care about our national interests. At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose,” he said.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump says the US will 'win' its war with Iran'very soon' But he leaves open the possibility of renewed military strikes before the midterm elections. Iran's foreign minister says Tehran is prepared for a renewed conflict with Washington.

Article Title: Powerful nor’easter floods US Northeast, leaves over 100,000 without power
Article Text:
Tidal flooding reaches homes, as a strong nor'easter coastal storm batters the US northeast coast, in Hampton, New Hampshire, US

A powerful nor’easter continued to batter the US Northeast on Sunday, bringing coastal flooding, strong winds and dangerous surf from New Jersey to New England, while disrupting power supplies and air travel across the region.According news agency AP, the storm killed a New York City Housing Authority worker on Saturday after a falling tree struck the worker. More than 100,000 customers across the Northeast and mid-Atlantic were without power at various points, while coastal communities faced repeated flooding as the slow-moving storm lingered over the region.New Jersey was among the worst-hit areas, with low-lying coastal communities experiencing repeated flooding during successive high tides. Some parts of the state received more than 4 inches of rain since Friday, adding to the flood threat.In Sea Bright, a coastal community in New Jersey, residents and businesses dealt with rising water as another high tide brought fresh flooding. Officials warned that additional tidal flooding could occur as the storm continued to move slowly through the region.The storm also brought strong winds to parts of New York. On Long Island, trees and utility poles were knocked down, causing power outages and damaging property.The National Weather Service said the storm was expected to weaken, but warned that the threat from coastal flooding would continue. Another round of high tides could bring further flooding to parts of New Jersey and New York.The weather system also disrupted air travel. More than 250 flights were cancelled at Boston Logan International Airport by late Sunday morning, while wind gusts at the airport reached around 40 mph.In New York City, several inches of water covered streets in the Howard Beach neighbourhood. Other coastal communities across the Northeast also reported flooding as strong winds pushed seawater inland.The storm has revived memories of Superstorm Sandy, which devastated parts of the US east coast in 2012 and caused more than $60 billion in damage. However, the current nor’easter is not comparable to Sandy in terms of overall impact, AP reported.Residents in some New Jersey communities said measures introduced after Sandy, including raising homes and using sandbags, helped limit damage from the latest storm.The nor’easter could also be the first of several major storms to affect the US east coast this fall, with meteorologists pointing to the influence of an El Niño weather pattern.
Article Summary: More than 100,000 customers across the Northeast and mid-Atlantic were without power at various points. New Jersey was among the worst-hit areas, with low- lying coastal communities experiencing repeated flooding during successive high tides. Some parts of the state received more than 4 inches of rain since Friday, adding to the flood threat.

Article Title: Talks with Iran likely to continue this week: Trump
Article Text:
President Donald Trump talks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House before boarding Marine One

US President Donald Trump said Sunday that he expects talks with Iran to resume this week, a day after rejecting a truce proposal put forward by Tehran. "They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," Trump told Axios. "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."Iran said Friday it had submitted a proposal to US to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, but Trump rejected it, asserting that Iranian leaders wanted the deal because "they are losing so badly". "They overplayed their hand," Trump said in the Axios interview published Sunday. Axios reported that indirect talks could take place Monday. The fresh negotiations would be conducted through Qatari mediators, Axios added.
Article Summary: Iran said Friday it had submitted a proposal to US to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Trump rejected it, asserting that Iranian leaders wanted the deal because "they are losing so badly" "They overplayed their hand," Trump said in the Axios interview published Sunday.

Article Title: 20-year-old Azerbaijani woman allegedly drugged, gang-raped in Pakistan's Lahore
Article Text:
Azerbaijani woman, 20, allegedly drugged and gang-raped in Lahore; 3 booked (AP file photo)

A 20-year-old woman from Azerbaijan was allegedly gang-raped by three men in Lahore after being taken to a flat in the Defence Housing Authority area, news agency PTI cited police on Sunday.The incident allegedly took place after the woman, who came to Pakistan from Baku for business, was taken to a cafe by two women late on September 25. Police said three men joined them at the cafe around 11 pm and later offered to drop them in their vehicle.Instead, the men allegedly took the Azerbaijani woman to a flat, where they gave her an intoxicating substance and sexually assaulted her, according to police.She was later left near Lahore's Ghazi Interchange. The suspects allegedly took her iPhone before abandoning her.Police officer Anjum Bashir said the woman had been staying in Lahore's Raiwind area since arriving in Pakistan more than two weeks ago.Police have registered a case against three men and identified the main accused. Raids are being conducted to arrest the suspects, while their names have also been placed on the stop list to prevent them from leaving the country.The vehicle allegedly used in the incident has been recovered from the house of a relative of the main accused, Bashir said.Investigators are also examining the role of the two women who allegedly took the victim to the cafe.The woman has undergone a medical examination and police have registered the case under relevant provisions of the Pakistan Penal Code.
Article Summary: Azerbaijani woman, 20, allegedly drugged and gang-raped in Lahore; 3 booked. Incident allegedly took place after the woman was taken to a cafe by two women. Police said three men joined them at the cafe and later offered to drop them in their vehicle.

Article Title: 'Don't go back like this': Pakistan minister's throat-cut gesture to Afghan journalist backfires - video
Article Text:
Pak minister’s throat-cut gesture to Afghan journalist

Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif has faced criticism on social media over a threat-like gesture he made towards an Afghan woman journalist who questioned him about Pakistan's ties with the Taliban and its response to the treatment of Afghan women.The incident took place on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York.The video clearly shows that journalist asked Asif what message Pakistan had for the Taliban over their policies toward Afghan women and why Islamabad had not challenged those policies when the Taliban were considered friends."What's your message to the Taliban now? To change their policy towards Afghan women? Why at the beginning, Pakistan didn't teach them that," the journalist asked, according to a video of the exchange shared on social media.Asif interrupted her without answering the question and pointed towards her attire."Don't go back like this over there. They will... otherwise they will..," he said, while making a hand gesture across his neck.The gesture drew strong condemnation online, with several social media users saying it appeared to imply that the journalist could be killed if she returned to Afghanistan. Users also criticised Asif and the men accompanying him for laughing after his remarks.A user on X wrote: "This is an utterly disgraceful way for a senior government minister to respond to a woman asking a serious question.""A woman asking about the suffering of Afghan women deserved an answer not intimidation, mockery, and laughter," he added.The journalist's question centred on the Taliban's policies towards Afghan women and Pakistan's position on them. Social media users said the response and the gesture were inappropriate and appeared to carry a threat of violence.The incident comes amid fresh tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan, with Islamabad carrying out aerial and drone strikes inside Afghanistan early Thursday.The Taliban also confirmed to news agency Reuters that 28 "fighters" were killed after crossing from Pakistan into eastern Afghanistan. The ruling-authority in Kabul also added that most of them were former Afghan security personnel.Pakistan called the strikes as "precision attacks" on 10 locations. Federal information minister Atauallah Tarar said the operation was carried out in response to drones launched from Afghanistan a day earlier.According to Dawn, Tarar said in a post on X that the strikes targeted locations allegedly used for launching and storing drones. He described the operation as "deliberate, precise, calibrated and proportionate and strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan".Afghanistan has warned Pakistan of "dire consequences" over the strikes, describing them as blatant aggression."In this criminal aggression, four of our fellow Afghan compatriots have been martyred. The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan strongly condemns these blind and cowardly attacks in the harshest terms, considering them a flagrant violation of all principles, a blatant aggression, and a crime," Afghan government spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid said.Cross-border hostilities between the two neighbours have continued in recent weeks, with Pakistan carrying out military action, including aerial strikes, inside Afghanistan.
Article Summary: Pak defence minister Khawaja Asif made a threat-like gesture to an Afghan journalist. The journalist asked him about Pakistan's ties with the Taliban and its response to the treatment of Afghan women. Social media users said the response and the gesture were inappropriate and appeared to carry a threat of violence.

Article Title: At least 13 dead in suicide bomb blast near police post in northwestern Pakistan
Article Text:
Also Read:

Pakistani Taliban claims responsibility

Poll Vote & Share your view What is the most important action the government should take in response to the recent attack? Increase security at checkpoints Strengthen military operations Enhance community awareness programs Focus on diplomacy with militant groups 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

(With AP inputs)

At least 13 people were killed and around 35 others wounded on Saturday when a suicide bomber detonated an explosives-laden vehicle at a roadside police checkpoint in northwestern Pakistan, police and rescue officials said.The attack took place in Dera Ismail Khan, a district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. Local police chief Safdar Baloch said most of the injured were security personnel and passersby, with some in critical condition.According to Baloch, gunmen later opened fire on an ambulance carrying victims to a nearby hospital, killing a rescue worker and injuring two others.Two women and a child were also among those killed in the suicide bombing, he added.The Pakistan i Taliban, or Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility for the attack. The TTP is separate from, but allied with, the Afghan Taliban, which returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021 after the US withdrew its troops.Pakistan has witnessed a surge in militant attacks in recent years, many of them claimed by the TTP and the outlawed Baloch Liberation Army (BLA), a separatist group primarily active in neighbouring Balochistan province.Islamabad has repeatedly accused the Afghan Taliban of allowing TTP members to operate from Afghan soil and have demanded that Kabul prevent cross-border attacks into Pakistan. Afghan authorities have denied allowing their territory to be used for attacks against other countries.Dera Ismail Khan is near South Waziristan, a former militant stronghold where the Pakistani military has carried out several operations in recent years.In December 2023, a suicide bomber detonated an explosives-laden vehicle at the main gate of a police station in Dera Ismail Khan, killing at least 23 security personnel in one of the deadliest attacks in the area. It was claimed by Tehreek-e-Jihad Pakistan, a small militant group believed to be an offshoot of the TTP.
Article Summary: The attack took place in Dera Ismail Khan, a district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. The Pakistan i Taliban, or Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility. The TTP is separate from, but allied with, the Afghan Taliban.

Article Title: Pakistan govt puts Islamabad on lockdown as Imran Khan’s party pushes ahead with march
Article Text:
Islamabad locked down as PTI prepares for Imran Khan march

Leaders of former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan ’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party have vowed to press ahead with nationwide demonstrations demanding his release, as authorities tightened security in Islamabad ahead of the planned march.More than 1,000 shipping containers, many reinforced with spikes, have been placed to block roads, while sandbags have been positioned on bridges and a key highway leading into the capital has been closed. Public gatherings have also been banned in Islamabad, with 22,000 police and other security personnel deployed across the city.The government has also deployed security personnel in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and closed the main highway linking the provincial capital, Peshawar, with Islamabad. The sweeping security measures have fuelled anger and frustration in the capital, with several businesses struggling to receive supplies.The measures to prevent Khan’s PTI from proceeding with the march come amid mounting concerns over the treatment of the former prime minister, who has been in jail since August 2023 following convictions in multiple cases.On Friday, PTI leaders announced that they would postpone the start of the march to October 4, a week after the original September 27 date, saying they hoped the delay would put further pressure on the government.The planned protest also comes amid the detention of three of Imran Khan’s sisters. Aleema Khan was detained last week, followed by Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, who were ordered to remain in custody for 30 days under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance.
Article Summary: More than 1,000 shipping containers, many reinforced with spikes, have been placed to block roads. Sandbags have been positioned on bridges and a key highway leading into the capital has been closed. Public gatherings have also been banned in Islamabad, with 22,000 police and other security personnel deployed.

Article Title: Pakistan goes bananas over giant gorillas dancing to Bollywood songs
Article Text:
Clips of these larger-than-life performers have been spreading rapidly online (Photo: AFP)

Pakistanis are going bananas over a trend that has crossed the Indian border: Giant gorillas, dancing to Bollywood music.Clips of these larger-than-life performers have been spreading rapidly online, turning them into the surprise stars of weddings, birthdays and other festivities.In the videos, guests can be seen joining in alongside the costumed entertainers, many of them visibly delighted by the unusual addition to their celebrations. The performers swing their oversized arms to pounding DJ tracks while partygoers gather round and dance, creating a lively, comic spectacle that has quickly drawn attention across social media.Behind the trend in Lahore is Shayen Zahoor, who runs Gorilla.co.pk, a business offering giant dancing gorilla acts for events across the city.Speaking to AFP, Zahoor explained how quickly the idea took off. He said the costume was ordered in early April and arrived by the end of the same month, after which the team wasted no time putting it to use.Once the suit arrived, he and his team lost no time getting started."We uploaded a reel on Instagram, and within just two days it reached a million views," Zahoor recalled.The overwhelming response convinced them to treat the venture as a serious business, and bookings soon began pouring in, with the public reaction proving remarkably enthusiastic."On the very first day, we received approximately 1,200 to 1,300 messages," he said, describing how curious would-be customers flooded his inbox.Many wanted to know whether the costume had genuinely arrived, what it would cost to book, and other practical details before making up their minds.What began as a single Instagram reel has since snowballed into a full-fledged entertainment phenomenon, with giant gorillas now a familiar, if unlikely, fixture at Pakistani celebrations.
Article Summary: Giant dancing gorillas have become a popular feature at Pakistani celebrations. The performers swing their oversized arms to pounding DJ tracks while partygoers gather round. A single Instagram reel has since snowballed into a full-fledged entertainment phenomenon. The trend has even crossed the Indian border.

Article Title: Pakistan govt crackdown forces PTI retreat? Imran's party likely to postpone Sept 27 Islamabad march
Article Text:
Imran Khan has been in jail since 2023

Pakistan minister says PTI has 'run away'

(With PTI inputs)

The Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) has decided to postpone its planned march to Islamabad from September 27 to October 4, party insiders said on Friday.The PTI had planned the march to the capital to demand the release of its incarcerated founder and former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan . The decision to delay the protest apparently came in response to the tough measures taken by the federal government to prevent it.According to PTI sources, the decision was taken at a party meeting and will be formally announced by Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister and PTI leader Sohail Afridi.Earlier in the day, Afridi had asserted at a press conference in Peshawar that the planned long march would go ahead despite road blockades and other measures. However, he expressed concern over reports of nails being driven into roads at the provincial boundaries, questioning whether a conspiracy to “cut” Khyber Pakhtunkhwa off from the rest of Pakistan had formally begun.“Our long march will definitely take place. This time, we will definitely come out. Put nails on the roads, place containers or fire bullets, we will come out. We will end this corrupt system of fake rulers,” he told reporters.“Pakistan will not break at any cost and we will save Pakistan,” he added.Cricketer-turned-politician Khan, 73, has been held at Rawalpindi’s high-security Adiala Jail since 2023, when he was arrested following his conviction in a corruption case.Pakistan information minister Ataullah Tarar reacted to the reports by saying the PTI had “run away” because it had made “no preparations” for the march to Islamabad.“There are no preparations for the PTI’s long march either, and that is why they have backed out of this protest. If they have the courage, let them come and hold the march,” Tarar said.The federal government had placed shipping containers along Islamabad’s main roads, allowing them to be closed at short notice ahead of the planned march.Hotels in the Faizabad area of Rawalpindi had been closed, while restaurants and shopkeepers were directed to shut their businesses. Guest houses and transport terminals in Faizabad had also been ordered to close from Friday night.Thousands of security personnel were deployed in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, the capital’s twin city and home to Pakistan Army headquarters, to control Khan’s supporters.Tensions over the planned protest continued despite PTI chairman Gohar Ali Khan urging the government to open negotiations and warning against confronting political workers with force.
Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) has decided to postpone its planned march to Islamabad from September 27 to October 4. The PTI had planned the march to the capital to demand the release of its founder and former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan. Khan has been held at Rawalpindi’s high-security Adiala Jail since 2023, when he was arrested following his conviction in a corruption case.

Article Title: 'Could endanger his life': Imran Khan's son warns against Adiala jail protest
Article Text:
Imran Khan's son warns against Adiala jail protest

Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan 's son Kasim Khan has urged Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters not to march towards Rawalpindi's Adiala jail during the party's planned September 27 protest, warning that such a move could be used by Pakistani authorities as a pretext for a "counter" assault on the prison and put his father's life at risk.The warning comes ahead of the PTI's planned protest and march, which is being held to demand Imran Khan's release.The former premier has been in prison since August 2023 following convictions in multiple cases.In a post on X, Kasim said he had been asked to appeal to supporters against gathering near Adiala jail."I’ve been instructed to call on the public not to attempt to march or protest nearby Adiala jail on 27. I’ve heard from sources that this may be used as an excuse for the establishment to launch a “counter” assault on the jail (Which my father is being held in), which could endanger his life. Please do not give them any reasons for “accidents” to happen to my father during the protest," Kasim's post read.His appeal comes as security measures have been stepped up across Punjab ahead of the PTI mobilisation.The Punjab government has imposed Section 144 across the province from September 23 to October 5, restricting public gatherings of five or more people on roads and in public places. Authorities have also sought the deployment of Pakistan Rangers in Rawalpindi, Attock, Jhelum and Mianwali.The restrictions have been imposed citing security concerns. A provincial notification referred to a "serious and imminent threat" to public peace and safety from militant and terrorist organisations and hostile intelligence agencies.The planned protest comes amid the detention of three of Imran Khan's sisters. Aleema Khan was detained last week, followed by Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, who were detained for 30 days under the Punjab maintenance of public order ordinance.On Thursday, the Lahore high court refused to immediately suspend the detention orders against Uzma and Noreen. The court issued notices to the respondents and sought their replies before taking up the plea further.The detentions have added to tensions ahead of the September 27 mobilisation.According to Dawn, lawyers for Uzma and Noreen told the Lahore high court that the two women were "non-political" and had been detained without sufficient legal justification. The court decided to wait for the authorities' response before ruling on their request to suspend the detention orders.Kasim had earlier criticised the detention of his aunts and other relatives and called for international attention to the issue.“This is a disgrace. Now my Aunts Dr. Uzma and Noreen, along with my cousins Shershah and Shahrez, have now been abducted as well. They have broken into my aunties' and cousins' houses and forced them into vehicles with no explanation. No reasons for arrest have been stated," he said in a post on X.Pakistani authorities have said the preventive detentions and restrictions are linked to public-order and security concerns. The Punjab government's notification specifically cited threats from militant organisations and other security risks while announcing the province-wide restrictions.The September 27 PTI protest is expected to add to the political and security pressure surrounding Imran Khan's continued incarceration, with authorities tightening restrictions and increasing security in areas linked to the planned mobilisation.
Article Summary: Kasim Khan urges supporters not to march towards Rawalpindi's Adiala jail during the party's planned September 27 protest. He warns that such a move could be used as a pretext for a "counter" assault on the prison and put his father's life at risk. Security measures have been stepped up across Punjab ahead of the protest.
